Delarbre * ''Cerasus racemosa'' Gray * ''Druparia padus'' (L.) Clairv. * ''Padus avium'' Mill. * ''Padus racemosa'' C.K.Schneid. * ''Prunus padus'' var. ''racemosa'' Domin * ''Prunus racemosa'' Lam. }} }} |synonyms_ref = }} '''''Prunus padus''''', the '''bird cherry''', is a [[flowering plant]] in the [[Rosaceae|rose family]], the type species of the subgenus ''[[Prunus subg. Padus|Padus]]'', which have [[flower]]s in [[raceme]]s. It is native to [[Europe]] and [[North Asia|northern]] and [[northeast Asia]]. == Distribution == ''Prunus padus'' is native to temperate Eurasia from the British Isles to Japan.{{cite web|title=''Prunus padus'' L. |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |work=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:730076-1 |access-date=17 March 2024}} Its distribution includes all Western and Central Europe north of the [[Pyrenees]] and the [[Alps]] and south of the [[Tree line|treeline]] with small pockets also found in [[Iberian Peninsula|Iberia]] and [[Northern Italy]] and in the [[Atlas Mountains]] of [[North Africa]]. It also inhabits all of [[Eastern Europe]] north of the [[Balkan Mountains]] and the [[Steppe]], as well as in the [[Caucasus]]. In Asia it is found throughout the forests of [[Siberia]], [[Mongolia]], [[Russian Far East|the Russian Far East]], northernmost [[Korea]], [[Hokkaido]], and northeastern [[China]].{{cite journal |last=Nestby |first=Rolf D. J. |title=The Status of ''Prunus padus'' L. (Bird Cherry) in Forest Communities throughout Europe and Asia |journal=Forests |volume=11 |issue=5 |date=2020-04-29 |issn=1999-4907 |doi=10.3390/f11050497 |doi-access=free |page=497|hdl=11250/2726335 |hdl-access=free }} It is an invasive species in Alaska, prompting efforts at eradication.Graziano, Gino. [https://www.uaf.edu/ces/publications/database/insects-pests/control-invasive-chokecherry.php Invasive Plant Issues: Control of Invasive Chokecherry Trees (Prunus padus and virginiana)], November 2020, ''Cooperative Extension Service, University of Alaska at Fairbanks''. Retrieved 5 May 2024. ==Description== It is a [[deciduous]] small [[tree]] or large [[shrub]] up to {{Convert|16|m|feet}}, rarely to 20 m tall, with a trunk up to 80 cm diameter. The leaves are alternate, 7–13 cm long and 4–7 cm broad, with finely serrated margins. It flowers in mid to late spring, typically late May in Britain; the flowers are produced on spreading or drooping racemes 7–15 cm long. The fruit is black when ripe, 8 mm diameter, with deciduous sepals; it is strongly [[astringent]] due to its [[tannin]] content.{{cite book |last=Rushforth |first=Keith D. |title=Trees of Britain and Europe |publisher=HarperCollins |publication-place=London |date=1999 |isbn=0-00-220013-9 |pages=1024–1025}}{{cite web|url=http://www-saps.plantsci.cam.ac.uk/trees/cherry.htm|publisher=Science & Plants for Schools (U.K.)|title=Bird cherry (''Prunus padus'')}} Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 12.8 days, and always bears a single seed per fruit. The fruit averages 78.4% water, and their [[dry matter|dry weight]] includes 31.3% [[carbohydrate]]s and 1.3% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}} There are two [[variety (botany)|varieties]]: * '''European bird cherry''' ''Prunus padus'' var. ''padus'', Europe and western Asia. * '''Asian bird cherry''' ''Prunus padus'' var. ''commutata'', eastern Asia. == Ecology == [[File:Apis mellifera - Prunus padus - Keila.jpg|thumb|left|Pollination]] [[Image:Prunus padus Tuomi marjoja VII 04 2989 C.JPG|thumb|Bird cherries ([[drupes]])]] [[File:Prunus padus Rauma.jpg|thumb|A bird cherry in full bloom]] The flowers are [[plant sexuality|hermaphroditic]] and pollinated by bees and flies. The fruit is readily eaten by [[bird]]s, which do not perceive astringency as unpleasant.{{cn|date=August 2024}} In Eurasia, the [[bird-cherry ermine]] moth (''Yponomeuta evonymella'') uses bird cherry as its host plant, and the larvae can eat single trees leafless.{{cite web |title=''Yponomeuta evonymella'' |website=UKmoths |url=https://www.ukmoths.org.uk/species/yponomeuta-evonymella/ |access-date=2026-07-13}} ==Poison== The [[glycoside]]s [[prulaurasin]] and [[amygdalin]], which can be poisonous to some mammals, are present in some parts of ''P. padus'', including the leaves, stems and fruit.{{ cite journal |url=http://veterinaryrecord.bmj.com/content/138/8/188.extract |journal=Veterinary Record |author=N.D.Sargison |author2=D.S.Williamson |author3=J.R.Duncan |author4=R.W.McCance |title=''Prunus padus'' (bird cherry) poisoning in cattle |year=1996 |volume=138 |issue=8 |page=188 |quote=...stems, leaves and fruits of ''P. padus'' contain the glycosides prulaurasin and amygdalin... |doi=10.1136/vr.138.8.188|pmid=8677622 |s2cid=43622812 |url-access=subscription }} == Cultivation and uses == The fruit of this tree is seldom used in western Europe, but, long ago, may possibly have been used as a food far to the east.{{citation needed|date=August 2024}} [[File:Bird cherry pie. Siberia.jpg|Bird cherry pie, Siberia|200px|thumb|right]]In Russia the fruit of the tree is still used for culinary purposes. The dried berries are milled into a flour of variable fineness that forms the principal ingredient of bird-cherry cake. The flour is brown, and so is the cake, even though there is no chocolate in it. Both flour and cake are sold in local stores and bakeries. In a more conventional method of preparation, fresh bird cherries may also be minced and cooked to make jam.{{cn|date=August 2024}} In North America bird cherry is grown as an [[ornamental tree]];{{Cite web |title=Prunus padus – Plant Finder |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=g980}} it is often attacked by the [[black knot]] fungus there.{{cn|date=August 2024}} The variety ''commutata'' is sold as an ornamental tree in North America under the common name mayday. It is valued for its hardiness and spring display of fragrant, white flowers.{{Cite web | url=http://www1.agric.gov.ab.ca/$department/deptdocs.nsf/all/agdex1000?opendocument |title = Agriculture and Forestry | date=22 August 2025 }} The common name mayday tree refers to the [[Beltane|May Day festival]], being unrelated to the [[Mayday|distress signal mayday]]. The name for the tree was in use prior to the adoption of "mayday" (the phonetic equivalent of the French {{Lang|fr|m'aider}} – from {{Lang|fr|venez m'aider}}, "come [and] help me") as an international distress signal.The London Journal: and Weekly Record of Literature, Science, and Art, Volume 32, page 475. ==History== According to [[Herodotus]] (writing around 2500 years ago) a strange race called the [[Argippaeans]], all bald from birth, who lived in an area identifiable possibly as the foothills of the [[Urals]], would pick the bean-sized fruits of a tree called "pontic" and squeeze from them a drinkable black juice, making afterwards, from the residue of the pressing, a type of cake. This juice and the "cakes" produced in its manufacture were, according to Herodotus (who derived his account from the reports of [[Scythian]] traders), the main sustenance of the "bald people". According to A. D. Godley, translator of an edition of the works of Herodotus published in the early 1920s, it was said that the [[Cossacks]] not only made a similar juice from ''Prunus padus'', but also called it by a name similar to the one (''aschu'') by which the bald Argippeans called theirs.{{cite web |url=https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Herodotus/4B*.html#23 |publisher=Loeb Classical Library at LacusCurtius |title=Herodotus, IV.23}} As might well be expected of so cherry-loving a race, the Argippeans – a just and kindly people – took good care of their trees, protecting them from the harsh winters of their homeland – seemingly by incorporating them (as a central pole symbolising the [[axis mundi]]) into the [[yurt]]-like felt tents in which they lived:
They dwell each man under a tree, covering it in winter with a white [[felt]] cloth, but using no felt in summer. These people are wronged by no man, for they are said to be sacred; nor have they any weapon of war. These are they who judge in the quarrels between their neighbours; moreover, whatever banished man has taken refuge with them is wronged by none.

— Herodotus, [[Histories (Herodotus)|Ἱστορίαι]] (''The Histories'') Book IV, Chapter 23
== Culture == Other vernacular names that have been used for the species include hackberry (unrelated to the genus ''Celtis''),{{cn|date=August 2026}} hagberry,{{cn|date=August 2026}} and mayday. In [[Finland]] and [[Sweden]], the blooming of bird cherry (Finnish {{Lang|fi|tuomi}}, Swedish {{Lang|sv|hägg}}) signifies the start of the summer for many people. In southern Finland, this normally takes place during the two last weeks of May or very early June.{{cn|date=August 2024}} The Ukrainian song ''[[Cheremshyna]]'' refers to a blooming of bird cherry.{{cn|date=August 2024}} A taboo on the use of the wood of the bird cherry was reported by natives of [[Advie]], in northeast Scotland, who believed it to be a "witches' tree".[[Walter Gregor]], "[[s:The Folk-Lore Journal/Volume 7/Some Folklore of Trees, Animals, and River-fishing from the N.E. of Scotland|Some Folklore of Trees, Animals, and River-fishing from the N.E. of Scotland]]". ''The Folk-Lore Journal''. Volume 7, 1889. p. 41. The tree was used medicinally during the Middle Ages,{{clarify|what part? what use?|date=March 2011}} during which period it was also believed that the bark of the tree, placed at the door, would ward off [[Plague (disease)|plague]].{{clarify|in what time period?|date=March 2011}} Bird cherry, and the closely related [[chokecherry]] ''P. virginiana'', are abundant as introduced [[invasive species]] in Anchorage, Alaska, having been planted in great numbers by landscapers and homeowners. They displace native trees and are harmful to moose and to young salmon.Chauvet, Jen. "[https://kenaiinvasives.org/plants/chokecherry-alaskas-pretty-problem-plant/ Chokecherry: Alaska's Pretty Problem Plant]", ''Kenai Peninsula Cooperative Invasive Species Management'', 11 July 2022.
